nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the war story, the sardonic sketch and the tale of terror
literary_identity: Journalist, satirist and short-story writer; the author of The Devil's Dictionary and the greatest American short story of the Civil War.
biography: Born Ambrose Gwinnett Bierce in Meigs County, Ohio, on 24 June 1842; he served with the Union army in the Civil War from 1861, was wounded at Kennesaw Mountain, and worked as a journalist in San Francisco from 1867, becoming the most feared satirist on the Pacific coast. He wrote for Hearst's newspapers in the 1890s, published Tales of Soldiers and Civilians in 1891 and The Devil's Dictionary in 1906, and disappeared in Mexico in 1913 while following Pancho Villa's army; his fate is unknown.
literary_profile: Bierce wrote the American story of war and terror with a cold precision unmatched in his century: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' and 'Chickamauga' are the finest American stories about the Civil War, and their technique — the twist of perspective, the delayed revelation, the ironic reversal — is the foundation of the modern short story. His Devil's Dictionary is the great American work of satire, and his ghost stories are among the most effective in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: The short, precisely engineered story with a reversed or delayed ending; the ironic narration that gives nothing away; the sensory immediacy of pain and fear; the sardonic epigram and definition; the unexplained supernatural event.
intellectual_concerns: War, death and the illusion of escape; the supernatural and the uncanny; the folly and hypocrisy of society; journalism and the corruption of the press; the military mind and the machinery of command.
historical_significance: Bierce is the central American writer of the short story of terror and the founder of the modern ironic short story: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' is one of the most anthologised stories in American literature, The Devil's Dictionary is a permanent American classic, and his technique shaped the short story from O. Henry to Borges.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Middle Border story and the literature of agrarian protest
literary_identity: Novelist, essayist and reformer; the founder of the American realistic story of the farm and the chronicler of the Middle Border.
biography: Born Hannibal Hamlin Garland at West Salem, Wisconsin, on 14 September 1860, the son of a homesteader; he taught school, homesteaded in Dakota, and went to Boston in 1884 to study and lecture. Main-Travelled Roads (1891) made him the spokesman of the western farmer; he campaigned for the Populist Party, wrote the 'Middle Border' memoirs from 1917, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1922. He died in Hollywood on 4 March 1940.
literary_profile: Garland founded the American literature of the farm: Main-Travelled Roads is the first American story collection to tell the truth about the drudgery, debt and loneliness of midwestern farm life, and its revolt against the sentimental rural idyll made it the central literary document of the Populist movement. He was also the first American writer to theorise 'veritism', the doctrine that fiction should record the actual conditions of the ordinary life, and his Middle Border memoirs are a classic of American autobiography.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, documentary, unadorned prose; the single incident that reveals a life; dialect and the actual speech of the farm; the grey landscape and the unremitting labour; the political argument carried through the situation; the memoir of the ordinary family.
intellectual_concerns: The farm, debt and the single tax; the loneliness and drudgery of women on the prairie; Populism and the revolt of the farmer; the closing of the frontier; the Middle Border and the passing of the pioneer generation; the artist who escapes and the price of escape.
historical_significance: Garland is the founder of American agrarian realism and the central literary voice of the Populist revolt: Main-Travelled Roads changed the American picture of the farm for ever, his 'veritism' was the American version of naturalist doctrine, and his Middle Border books are among the great American memoirs of the westward movement.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Under the Wheel (play, 1890); Main-Travelled Roads (1891); Jason Edwards: An Average Man (1892); A Little Norsk (1892); A Spoil of Office (1892); Prairie Folks (1893); Crumbling Idols (1894); Rose of Dutcher's Coolly (1895); Wayside Courtships (1897); The Spirit of Sweetwater (1898); The Trail of the Goldseekers (1899); Boy Life on the Prairie (1899); Her Mountain Lover (1901); The Captain of the Gray-Horse Troop (1902); Hesper (1903); The Tyranny of the Dark (1905); The Shadow World (1908); Cavanagh, Forest Ranger (1910); A Son of the Middle Border (1917); A Daughter of the Middle Border (1921); Trail-Makers of the Middle Border (1926); Back-Trailers from the Middle Border (1928).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the local-colour story of Louisiana and the literature of racial justice
literary_identity: Novelist and essayist; the first American writer to make New Orleans and the Creole South the subject of serious fiction, and a lifelong campaigner for racial equality.
biography: Born in New Orleans on 12 October 1844, the son of a slaveholding family ruined by the Civil War; he served in the Confederate cavalry, and after the war worked as a clerk and surveyor before publishing Old Creole Days in 1879. He became the most outspoken white southern advocate of civil rights in the 1880s, moved to Massachusetts in 1885, and wrote a series of novels on Louisiana life and history. He died at St Petersburg, Florida, on 31 January 1925.
literary_profile: Cable invented the American local-colour story of the deep South: his Old Creole Days and The Grandissimes record the speech, the courtyards, the manners and the racial complexity of French Louisiana with a precision no northern writer could imitate, and his essays of the 1880s were the most courageous white southern defence of black civil rights in the period. He was also the first American novelist to treat the legacy of slavery and the mixing of the races as the central moral problem of southern life.
stylistic_characteristics: Exact reproduction of Creole and black dialect; the vivid set piece of courtyard, market and street; the story told through a frame and a remembered voice; the sharp analysis of racial and class difference; the historical romance reconstructed from old New Orleans.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, emancipation and the unfinished work of Reconstruction; the Creole inheritance and the mixing of races; New Orleans and the Mississippi; the corruption of the Reconstruction governments; the moral responsibility of the white southerner; the literature of regional memory.
historical_significance: Cable is the founder of the Southern local-colour school and the most important white southern literary voice for racial justice in the nineteenth century: Old Creole Days and The Grandissimes created the literary image of New Orleans, and his civil-rights essays cost him his southern audience while making him a central figure in the American literature of race.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Old Creole Days (1879); The Grandissimes: A Story of Creole Life (1880); Madame Delphine (1881); Dr Sevier (1884); The Creoles of Louisiana (1884); The Silent South (1885); Bonaventure: A Prose Pastoral of Acadian Louisiana (1888); Strange True Stories of Louisiana (1889); The Negro Question (1890); John March, Southerner (1894); Strong Hearts (1899); The Cavalier (1901); Bylow Hill (1902); Kincaid's Battery (1908); Gideon's Band (1914); The Amateur Garden (1914); Lovers of Louisiana (1918).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England village story and the literature of women's lives
literary_identity: Short-story writer and novelist; the finest American regionalist of the New England village and the great chronicler of unmarried and widowed women.
biography: Born Mary Eleanor Wilkins at Randolph, Massachusetts, on 31 October 1852, into a strict Congregational family that lost its money; she attended Mount Holyoke Female Seminary for a year and began writing to support herself and her family. A Humble Romance (1887) and A New England Nun (1891) made her reputation; she married Dr Charles Freeman in 1902 and moved to New Jersey, where she wrote the novels and plays of her later years. She won the William Dean Howells Medal in 1926 and died at Metuchen, New Jersey, on 13 March 1930.
literary_profile: Freeman wrote the American story of the village woman: her subject is the unmarried daughter, the widow, the woman who keeps house for a man who does not notice her, and her method is the small, exact, almost cruel narrative in which a whole life is settled in a single afternoon. A New England Nun is one of the great American stories, and her novels Pembroke and The Shoulders of Atlas extend her vision to the whole village economy of New England.
stylistic_characteristics: Small-scale, tightly plotted narrative with a single decisive turn; exact rendering of New England dialect and domestic detail; the withheld epiphany; ironic comedy that edges into tragedy; the interior of the village house; the dignity and the narrowness of women's lives.
intellectual_concerns: Unmarried women, spinsterhood and the economics of the village household; marriage and the marriage market; women's work and women's property; the decay of rural New England; poverty and pride; the small cruelties of community.
historical_significance: Freeman is the finest American regionalist of the New England village and one of the great American writers of women's lives: A New England Nun is a permanent classic, her portrait of the unmarried woman is unique in nineteenth-century American fiction, and her work has become central to the feminist criticism of American literature.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the Creole short story, the lyric and the essay of the colour line
literary_identity: Poet, short-story writer, journalist and activist; the first African-American woman to publish a collection of short stories and a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance generation.
biography: Born Alice Ruth Moore in New Orleans on 19 July 1875, of mixed African, European and Native American descent; she taught school in New Orleans and Boston and published Violets and Other Tales in 1895. She married the poet Paul Laurence Dunbar in 1898; after their separation she taught at Howard High School in Wilmington, Delaware, wrote for the black press, and was active in the suffrage and anti-lynching movements. She died in Philadelphia on 3 September 1935.
literary_profile: Dunbar-Nelson wrote the African-American story of Creole New Orleans and the essay of the colour line: The Goodness of St Rocque is the first collection of stories by a black American woman, and its portraits of Creole life, of passing and of the colour hierarchy within black society are unmatched in the period. Her journalism, her diary and her suffrage essays make her a central figure in the transition from the literature of uplift to the Harlem Renaissance.
stylistic_characteristics: Dialect and French-inflected Creole speech; the short lyric sketch with a turn of irony; the diary as literary form; the essay of political argument; the rendering of the complex gradations of colour and class within black New Orleans.
intellectual_concerns: Race, colour and the Creole hierarchy; passing and the colour line; lynching and racial violence; women's suffrage and black women's activism; love and marriage; the literature of the New Negro.
historical_significance: Dunbar-Nelson is the first African-American woman to publish a book of short stories and a key figure in the literature of the colour line: The Goodness of St Rocque is a landmark of African-American fiction, her diary is a major document of black women's intellectual life, and her activism links the nineteenth-century reform movements to the Harlem Renaissance.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Violets and Other Tales (1895); The Goodness of St Rocque and Other Stories (1899); Mine Eyes Have Seen (play, 1918); The Dunbar Speaker and Entertainer (editor, 1920); The Works of Alice Dunbar-Nelson (3 vols, 1988, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Chinese-British-American; the Chinese-American short story and the literature of the immigrant
literary_identity: Journalist and short-story writer; the first Chinese-American writer of fiction in English and the great chronicler of Chinese immigrant life in America.
biography: Born Edith Maude Eaton at Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 15 March 1865, the daughter of an English silk merchant and a Chinese mother; the family emigrated to Montreal in 1872, and she worked as a stenographer and journalist, moving to San Francisco in 1898 and to Boston in 1912. She published stories under the name Sui Sin Far from 1890, collected in Mrs Spring Fragrance (1912), and died in Montreal on 7 May 1914.
literary_profile: Sui Sin Far wrote the first fiction in English about the Chinese in America: her stories of San Francisco's Chinatown and of the Chinese-American household record the immigrant experience from inside, with sympathy for both the Chinese and the white characters, and refuse the stereotypes of the yellow-peril press. Mrs Spring Fragrance is the founding text of Asian-American literature, and her journalism and essays make her the first important Asian-American literary voice.
stylistic_characteristics: The short story with a domestic interior and a small crisis; realistic dialogue across languages; the mixed-race perspective of a narrator who belongs to both worlds; gentle irony at the expense of white misunderstanding; the precise material detail of immigrant life.
intellectual_concerns: Chinese immigration and exclusion; the Chinese-American family and the arranged marriage; race, law and the immigrant; the encounter of East and West; mothering and childhood across cultures; the prejudice of the American press.
historical_significance: Sui Sin Far is the first Chinese-American writer of fiction and the founder of Asian-American literature: Mrs Spring Fragrance introduced the Chinese immigrant to American fiction as a human being rather than a stereotype, and her work is now recognised as a foundational text of Asian-American and multiracial American literature.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Mrs Spring Fragrance and Other Writings (1912); 'Leaves from the Mental Portfolio of an Eurasian' (1909); 'The Chinese in America' (1909); Mrs Spring Fragrance and Other Writings (expanded edition, 1995).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jewish-American; the immigrant novel and the Yiddish-American newspaper
literary_identity: Journalist, novelist and socialist; the founding editor of the Jewish Daily Forward and the author of The Rise of David Levinsky.
biography: Born in Podberezhie in the Russian Empire (now Belarus) on 7 July 1860; he studied at the Vilna Teachers' Institute, emigrated to the United States in 1882, and worked in a factory and as a teacher before founding the Jewish Daily Forward in 1897, which he edited until his death. His novel Yekl (1896) was the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant, and The Rise of David Levinsky (1917) is the classic American immigrant novel. He died in New York on 31 August 1951.
literary_profile: Cahan created the American immigrant novel: Yekl and The Rise of David Levinsky take the Jewish immigrant from the shtetl to the Lower East Side and to wealth, and record the cost of Americanisation with an honesty that no later immigrant writer has surpassed. He was also the greatest figure in Yiddish-American journalism, and the Forward under his editorship was the central institution of Jewish immigrant life in America.
stylistic_characteristics: Documentary realism with a precise record of work and wages; dialogue rendered in the mixed English of the immigrant; the ironic narrator who understands both the old world and the new; the rise-and-fall structure of the American success story; the analysis of assimilation as loss.
intellectual_concerns: Immigration and Americanisation; the Jewish shtetl and the Lower East Side; the garment trade and sweated labour; socialism and the labour movement; money and the cost of success; the immigrant family and generational conflict.
historical_significance: Cahan is the founder of the Jewish-American novel and the central figure of Yiddish-American journalism: The Rise of David Levinsky is the greatest American immigrant novel, Yekl is the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant, and the Forward made him the most influential Jewish voice in America.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto (1896); The Imported Bridegroom and Other Stories (1898); The Rise of David Levinsky (1917); Bletter fun Mayn Leben (5 vols, 1926-31); The Education of Abraham Cahan (1969, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the naturalist novel of the city and the literature of American desire
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of Sister Carrie and An American Tragedy, and the most thoroughgoing American naturalist.
biography: Born Herman Theodore Dreiser in Terre Haute, Indiana, on 27 August 1871, the ninth child of a devout German Catholic immigrant family; he was a newspaper reporter in Chicago, St Louis and Pittsburgh in the 1890s, and Sister Carrie was published in 1900 only after the publisher's wife objected to it. He worked as an editor of women's magazines until 1910, published Jennie Gerhardt and The Financier in 1911-12, and became the leading figure of American naturalism. He joined the Communist Party in 1945 and died in Hollywood on 28 December 1945.
literary_profile: Dreiser wrote the American naturalist novel of desire: Sister Carrie follows a young woman's rise in the city through the men who desire her, and An American Tragedy follows a young man's fall, both with a patient accumulation of detail and an absence of moral judgement that was new in American fiction. He was a clumsy stylist and a great novelist, and his refusal to condemn his characters made him the central American writer of the naturalist tradition and the model for the American novel of the twentieth century.
stylistic_characteristics: Slow accumulation of documentary detail; the flat, unhurried sentence; the interior of the city street, the hotel and the factory; the analysis of motive in biological and social terms; the refusal of authorial judgement; the long novel of a whole life.
intellectual_concerns: Desire, money and the American city; the woman who rises and the man who falls; poverty and the fear of poverty; the class system and the machinery of success; crime, guilt and the law; the determinism of heredity and environment.
historical_significance: Dreiser is the central American naturalist and one of the founders of modern American fiction: Sister Carrie and An American Tragedy are permanent classics, his refusal of moral judgement changed the American novel, and his influence on Fitzgerald, Faulkner, Richard Wright and the whole twentieth-century American novel is decisive.
